question: The family-owned publishing house 4 Kavky developed two dozen board games over five years and sold around 15,000 units. But it no longer exists today. The company was brought to its knees by extremely cheap Chinese copies that flooded the Chinese online marketplace Temu.

Anonymous sellers disappeared and returned under new profiles, they used stolen photos and descriptions, and sold these copies at prices that were not supported by costs. It didn’t help that the company had an extensive international licensing agreement. How can a company effectively defend itself in such a situation?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.2.2026) The sale of goods infringing intellectual property rights (IPR) is a serious challenge posed by the rise of e-commerce in the EU, with significant negative impact on consumers’ health and safety, innovation, small businesses and EU competitiveness1.

Online marketplaces operating in the EU must comply with horizontal and specific obligations under the Digital Services Act (DSA)2, such as putting in place user-friendly mechanisms to flag illegal content and appeal content moderation decisions and ensuring trader traceability.

Platforms designated as very large online platforms and very large online search engines are subject to additional obligations, including the assessment and mitigation of systemic risks related to illegal content, consumer protection, public health, protection of minors, etc.

Following its in-depth investigations opened in 20243, the Commission preliminarily found in June 2025 AliExpress to be in breach of its obligations to assess and mitigate risks related to the dissemination of illegal products4. The Commission also preliminarily found in July 20255 Temu to be in breach of its obligation to properly assess the risks of illegal products being disseminated on its marketplace.

If the Commission’s preliminary views are ultimately confirmed, it will adopt a non-compliance decision, possibly entailing fines6. Moreover, EU law provides different tools for rightsholders to protect their IPR and compete fairly in the digital marketplace.

Under Directive 2004/48/EC7, companies affected by counterfeiting may apply for an injunction against infringers and any intermediary whose services are being used to facilitate those infringements, including online platforms, to stop the infringing activities.
1 In 2025, the Commission set out a comprehensive approach in its E-commerce Communication to tackle the

dissemination of illegal goods online: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/e-commercecommunication-comprehensive-eu-toolbox-safe-and-sustainable-e-commerce. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng. 3 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_24_1485; https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_24_5622. 4 https://ec.europa.
